panels.speaker: pip
panels.text: Look at these apples. Someone has lined them up in neat rows.

panels.speaker: pip
panels.text: There are 3 rows. Each row has 4 apples in it.

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: You could count every apple one by one… but that is slow, and it is easy to lose your place.

panels.speaker: pip
panels.text: Instead, add one row at a time: 4, then 8, then 12.

panels.speaker: pip
panels.text: So 3 rows of 4 is 12. That is what an array does — it turns counting into adding.

question.prompt: This array has 2 rows of 5. How many altogether?

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: Nicely done. Rows of the same size are the whole trick.

title: What a Fraction Really Is
blurb: Equal parts, and why the bottom number matters.

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: Here is one whole chocolate bar.

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: Now I have snapped it into 4 equal pieces. Equal is the important word.

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: If I eat one piece, I have eaten 1 out of 4. We write that as 1/4.

panels.speaker: vex
panels.text: The bottom number says how many pieces the whole was cut into. The top says how many you have.

question.prompt: This bar is cut into 8 equal pieces and 3 are shaded. What fraction is shaded?
question.explanation: 3 shaded pieces out of 8 equal pieces is 3/8.

panels.speaker: vex
panels.text: Here is the surprise: the MORE pieces you cut something into, the SMALLER each piece is.

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: So 1/2 is bigger than 1/8, even though 8 is the bigger number. That trips up nearly everyone once.

title: Ratios and the Unit Rate
blurb: Getting to 'per one' is almost always the move.

panels.speaker: vex
panels.text: A ratio compares two amounts. Four red marbles to six blue is written 4 : 6.

panels.speaker: vex
panels.text: Ratios scale. Double both sides and nothing changes about the mixture: 4 : 6 is the same as 8 : 12.

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: The most useful thing you can do with a ratio is find the UNIT rate — how much for exactly one.

panels.speaker: nim
panels.text: Six apples cost $3. Divide both by 6, and one apple costs 50¢. Now you can price any number of apples.

question.prompt: 5 identical notebooks cost $10. What does ONE notebook cost, in dollars?

panels.speaker: vex
panels.text: Once you know the price of one, every other question is just multiplication.

question.prompt: So what would 7 of those notebooks cost, in dollars?

panels.speaker: vex
panels.text: That is the whole method. Get to one, then scale up.
